draft.title: Positioning readers on ethical issues
card: An ethical issue is a question about right and wrong, such as whether a character should keep a secret or break a rule. Writers can lead readers to take a side on it.
A writer chooses which actions and events to put on the page. Showing a character helping a stranger can lead readers to approve of them.
A writer can leave out a character's reasons or a point of view. If readers never hear one side, they may judge that side more harshly.
Word choice carries a judgement. Calling a character "firm" can win approval, while "stubborn" or "ruthless" can lead readers to disapprove of the same act.
draft.remember: Writers can guide your view of right and wrong through what they show, what they leave out and the words they choose.

a.q: A writer tells a story about a boy who keeps a lost wallet. The writer only describes how hungry and scared he is, and never mentions the owner. How does this position readers?
opts: It may lead readers to sympathise with the boy
It may lead readers to blame the boy for the act
It shows the owner's side of the story fairly
It proves that keeping the wallet is legal
a.why: By showing only the boy's fear and leaving out the owner, the writer can lead readers to sympathise with him. The second option is tempting, but leaving out the owner removes the main reason to blame the boy.
a.clue: Think about whose side of the story readers get to see.

b.q: Two writers describe the same event: a manager closes a shop. One says she "abandoned" the staff. The other says she "made a hard decision". What is the main technique shaping readers' opinions?
opts: Word choice that carries a judgement
Showing the staff's actions in detail
b.why: The event is the same in both, but "abandoned" leads readers to disapprove and "made a hard decision" leads them to understand her. The difference lies in the words chosen. Neither description adds new events or leaves anything out.
b.clue: The event is the same. What changes?

a.best: It may lead readers to sympathise with the boy

b.best: Word choice that carries a judgement
